extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers; writers/readers of periodical moral/humorous essays
extracted.subtask_description: Writing short, character-driven, moralizing humorous essays in the Spectator/periodical tradition: vivid character sketches, anecdote-driven scenes, classical allusion, and gently satirical moral judgments delivered in a conversational first-person voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small singularities as foils to virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an individual's oddities or eccentricities so that they 'set off' rather than blemish his good qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show eccentric behavior (e.g., standing up in church to count the congregation, calling out a man during service) as charming quirks that illuminate the subject's underlying worth; convey that acquaintances interpret little singularities as foils to a person's character rather than as disqualifying faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character through social ritual and small actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Let routine public behaviors and rituals (church exit, bowing, enquiring after absentees) manifest status and personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete moments in communal settings (the sermon, the procession out of church, catechising-day rewards) to show relationships of authority, affection, or reprimand; these brief, observable actions communicate power, kindness, and local morals without direct exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast neighboring examples to highlight virtues and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Place two proximate characters or parishes in opposition (amiable patron vs. feuding squire and parson) to make moral and social lessons clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtapose harmonious and discordant cases so readers infer consequences (e.g., how parishioners' beliefs and conduct change in a parish where the squire and parson feud); contrasts do heavy lifting—show rather than tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate moral maxims with concrete exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: State a practical maxim (economy, moderation) and exemplify it through named characters (Laertes vs Irus) who embody shame-of-poverty and fear-of-poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use named, contrasted portraits to embody abstract principles: narrate their choices, consequences, and daily habits so readers can infer the recommended moderation or its perils; this grounds philosophy in everyday life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid anecdote and incident to produce comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use detailed, often comic anecdotes (courtroom bowing, hunting mishaps, lovesick behaviour) to generate humor and characterize subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sensory specifics and plot-like mini-incidents (a widow's bewitching eye; Sir Roger carving a name on trees; the hare spared by the hunts) so the comic impression is anchored in believable particulars rather than abstract ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use genteel irony and satiric elevation of trivial feats
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat small or absurd accomplishments with exaggerated seriousness to create gentle satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply lofty diction or solemn narration to petty exploits (e.g., a brass nail through a fox's nose described as a great exploit) to produce ironic amusement while keeping the tone affectionate, not vindictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance anecdote with moral reflection in narrator voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Mix first-person observation and light-hearted confession with general reflections on human nature and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a conversational, authoritative narrator who moves between reporting incidents and drawing larger lessons (on economy, exercise, or felicity); this creates intimacy and moral weight without pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame essays with classical epigraphs and learned allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Open (and sometimes close) with Latin or classical quotations and sprinkle references to authorities (Virgil, Horace, Pascal, Sydenham) to lend erudition and ironic contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use highbrow allusion as seasoning: the classical line sets a tone and creates witty interplay between learned maxim and country anecdote; the juxtaposition often heightens humor by contrasting lofty thought with rustic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend practical, specific rules as comic moral counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer concrete prescriptions (e.g., resolve a personal spending cap) phrased as maxims to live by; present them as both reasonable and mildly humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn advice into a memorable rule backed by examples; the concreteness (choose a sum you will not exceed) makes the counsel usable and produces a quietly comic effect when applied to characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with natural philosophy or medical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When praising or condemning habits (exercise, labour), invoke medical or scientific sources and mechanical metaphors to justify the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the bodily/mental mechanisms (body as 'system of tubes and glands', exercise ferments humours) and cite contemporary medical authorities (e.g., Sydenham, Medicina Gymnastica) to make the case persuasive yet gently comic by mixing learned theory with homely prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sound, rhythm, and sensory description for lively scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Render scenes (the hunt, the cry of hounds, echoes across hills) with auditory and visual detail to lift readers into the moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic noises and movement (the cry like bells, echoes, the Horn) and describe pack discipline and animal behavior to create an immersive, pleasurable scene that supports both admiration and amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice humane, benevolent satire rather than cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Shape humor so it reveals human foibles but preserves affection (Sir Roger spares the hare, rewards good catechising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow characters to appear fallible without being cruelly exposed; balance mockery with generosity—readers laugh with, not merely at, the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let character be shown by consistency of small details
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulate minor consistent details (trophies on the wall, habits of riding and enquiry after tenants) to build a credible, emblematic portrait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated, concrete motifs (horns on the wall, patched stable doors, habits at church) serve as shorthand for a life and value-system—use them to give depth and comic recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer learned jest (Latin epigrams, playful classical references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include short Latin epigrams or playful translations to add wit aimed at an educated readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-chosen epigram (e.g., Martial rendered) can encapsulate a comic truth about a lovesick character and reward readers who appreciate classical play; keep translations brisk and pointed.
